Collective Editorial Statement

As editors charged with showcasing exemplary works of eliterature from 2016-2021, we reviewed 450+ works, discussing each work multiple times over our three-year production process.

Building on editorial efforts in the three previous Collections, our five ELC4 editors centered Equity, Diversity and Inclusion (EDI) in our process. The result? 132 literary works from 42 author nationalities in 31 languages.

When we began in June 2019, we couldn’t have foreseen that the world would be upended by the COVID-19 pandemic nine months later. Lockdowns and universities’ sudden pivot to virtual learning affected our editorial processes. We adopted an entirely virtual workflow. We slowed our timeline. When all the world’s events moved online, we discovered new-to-us artists and actively recruited their participation in ELC4.

A sense of urgency and reckoning grew. We developed a shared conviction to revise the tradition of Electronic Literature Collections, unbinding expectations of modernist difficulty and rethinking authorship to include writing in participatory cultures where there’s no one “author.”

We learned that what might be classified as elit in one cultural tradition might not in another, which informed our evaluations. Eliterature is locally situated and culturally specific. Being a global collection means fostering heterogeneity. During editorial review, we revisited works to ensure consistent application of our criteria.

Centering Equity, Diversity and Inclusion [EDI]

ELC4 presents the largest and most diverse group yet of elit authors writing in Afrikaans, Ancient Chinese, Arabic, Catalan, Chinese, Danish, Dutch, English, French, German, Greek, Hungarian, Indonesian, isiXhosa, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Mezangelle, Norwegian, Polish, Portuguese, Romanian, Russian, Setswana, Simplified Chinese, Slovak, South African Sign Language, Spanish, Swedish, Turkish, Yoruba.

ELC4 is the first ELC offering access to some commercial works, such as VR experiences playable even without headsets, and narrative video games. These join the Collection’s far more numerous open access works: database fictions, autoethnographies by GenZ makers, works that play cleverly with AI, geospatial storytelling via mobile phones, and many more.

Our goal was to welcome artists who may never have heard of “elit” or encountered it in a classroom. We sought and found works by Indigenous makers from many cultures. We found new-to-elit makers by attending live streamed performances and virtual exhibits from makers in India, Mexico, and West Africa. Elit scholars in Chile, Argentina, and Brazil connected us with media artists in Central and South America. International consultants from Asia, the Middle East, eastern and western Europe, Australia, and Africa helped us find works imbued by their local cultures. International consultants wrote evaluations when we editors didn’t speak the languages.

ELC4 features many more BIPOC, queer, and female or female-identifying authors than in previous Collections, allowing us to interrogate our core beliefs about elit.

However, there is much more work yet to do in decentering patriarchal and imperial culture as the implied standard of elit.

Evolving Definitions

Although useful to understand and interpret literary corpora, definitions of elit are incomplete and evolving. Eliterature authors creatively adopt new technologies whenever available, eluding contemporaneous definitions. Works selected for ELC4 are varied, spreading beyond known genres, and challenging the previous perceptions of elit manifest in the three previous Collections.

Eliterature qualities derive meaning from a fusion of computational and literary layers. This fusion shows that human literary creativity entwines technological innovation with cultural and historic context. Eliterature works invite readers to engage with texts through embedded feedback mechanisms and often require traversing a network of potential paths.

A definition of elit must capture its hybrid permanent evolution, embracing new aesthetic forms. As we evaluated works, it became clear that the definition we published in our Call for Works in June 2019 required updating.

Some works we wanted to include defied the field’s definition of elit, prompting an ongoing, two-year conversation about how to represent the full corpora of elit works. All elit works involve interaction with technology, which can occur at any stage in the process from conception to reception. Elit works, to some degree or another, incorporate: (1) literary qualities co-produced by human and algorithmic interaction; (2) formal and/or conceptual innovation; (3) a transforming experience for readers through expressive algorithms.

We updated the glossary, establishing bridges to previous Collections and adding terms as warranted by new forms. Elit genres are themselves processual: transitional and descriptive rather than prescriptive. Aesthetic tension is constantly being torqued as artists explore the expressive limits of their writing tools.

Accessibility and Classification

Who uses the Electronic Literature Collection, and how do they use it? How might people use ELC4 in the future? These questions drove our website design and choices about what metadata to collect from authors.

An ELC is always an archive of elit from its own cultural moment. And yet it must also interoperate with databases such as the Electronic Literature Directory, the NEXT, Consortium of Electronic Literature, and Electronic Literature Knowledge Base [ELMCIP]. We reviewed the metadata schema of those systems and implemented a complementary system that could work with them. Where possible, we transferred into ELC4 metadata some elements from those systems, such as matching technical keywords and genres, to maximize continuity and discoverability.

We created and tracked tens of thousands of pieces of metadata using Google Forms and Sheets, the interactive whiteboard Miro, and Twine to build a metadata collection system. Most of this metadata is piped into the website you’re now reading.

Robust metadata empowers readers to re-arrange the collection to serve their own individual purposes. Video playthroughs allow readers to sample a work and see how to play it. Archived versions of each work guarantee perpetual access, even if it stops existing in the world beyond ELC4. Where possible, code and assets are shared so scholars and others can delve into what makes a work run.

Search is predictive in ELC4. Autocomplete will show whether the term exists as a keyword, and how many works carry the tag. Anyone can easily build unique subsets of works using keywords, powered by ELC4’s handbuilt search and filtering system.

Filters can be applied and combined across all categories, enabling increased refinement and inclusion. We hope that you will find, sift, and order the works in Volume 4 to suit your needs.

The order of the work tiles on the ELC4 home page are randomized, to ensure that no particular group of works is ever consistently less visible on the bottom of the page. On the other hand, this random order only changes every 24 hours, to allow instructors to share the same screen as students during a live class.

We have also added a toggle to the footer that enables an accessibility mode which will address common issues including the need for high contrast.

We identified the following keyword categories: Content, Genre, Technical, and Identity.

Content keywords convey the primary themes incorporated into the work, such as character, genre, political aspects, history, geography, and more. Authors provided these.

Genre keywords are unique to elit, both drawing from the rich history of eliterature traditions and scholarship, and helping to define emergent forms. Editors defined these in the Glossary.

Technical refers to programs, media, and coding languages. We further divide the technical category into three subcategories: Format, Platform, and Authoring Language, which includes the full variety of programming languages, APIs, and authoring tools used.

Identity is the most ethically thorny of the metadata we collected. We document these using subcategories, including nationality, creator keywords, and language. We collected Identity keywords, an element not present in previous Collections, because our commitment to EDI calls for accountability. We wanted to know, and enable the community to know, how inclusive ELC4 is and where it might need to improve.

We emphasize that identity tags are associated with individual works, not with individual authors. We left it up to authors to assign identity-based keywords to their works, or to not assign any Identity keywords at all. We editors would not employ a top-down approach. As such, the ELC4 does not purport to offer a definitive measure of the gender, sexuality, age, or dis/ability of its authors. It measures what authors chose to share. We anticipate this approach may change in subsequent Collections. We hope that future Collection editors will gather feedback about this approach and iterate their own EDI and metadata practices.

As our definition of elit evolved over three years working on this Collection, so too did our understanding of how elit authors invite readers to experience literature by playing with expressive algorithms. We hope the joy we felt making ELC4 is matched in your reading experience of it.

Biographies

Editors (Alphabetically)

Kathi Inman Berens (United States) is Associate Professor of Book Publishing and Digital Humanities at Portland State University. She authors book consumer behavioral research, and eliterary criticism. The U.S. Fulbright Scholar of Digital Culture in Norway 2014-5, Berens publishes in Digital Humanities Quarterly, Debates in Digital Humanities, electronic book review, Publishers Weekly, and other venues.

John T. Murray (United States) is Assistant Professor of Games and Interactive Media department at the University of Central Florida. He is co-author of Flash: Building the Interactive Web (MIT Press, 2014) and Adventure Games: Playing the Outsider (Bloomsbury, 2020). His research focuses on interactive narratives and reality media, which includes augmented, virtual and mixed reality.

R. Lyle Skains (New Mexico/Wales) is a Principal Academic in Health and Science Communication at Bournemouth University, conducting practice-based research into creating and publishing interactive digital narratives for scicomm. Monographs: Digital Authorship (Cambridge UP), Using Interactive Digital Narrative for Health and Science Education (Emerald), and forthcoming Neverending Stories: The Popular Emergence of Digital Fiction (Bloomsbury).

Rui Torres (Portugal) is Professor of Communication Sciences at University Fernando Pessoa, member of the NOVA Institute of Communication, director at the Electronic Literature Organization, editor of Cibertextualidades (UFP Press) and co-editor of the Electronic Literature Series (Bloomsbury), coordinator of the Digital Archive of Portuguese Experimental Poetry, and poet.

Mia Zamora (United States) is Professor of English and Director of the MA in Writing Studies at Kean University in Union, NJ. A Fulbright Scholar of Digital Culture in Norway 2017-8, her recent scholarship focuses on socially just care. She has founded the global learning networks Equity Unbound (#unboundeq) and Networked Narratives (#netnarr).

International Consultants

Agat (India) is a theatre maker and artist based in Amsterdam. He is a co-instigator of dra.ft.

Ambika Joshi (India) is Computational Mama, a designer and creative technologist. Her work explores coding as a form of self-care and learning. She is a co-instigator of dra.ft, which lives here - https://dra-ft.site/

Anna Nacher (Poland) is an associate professor at the Jagiellonian University, 2020 Fulbright scholar, an elit curator, and a member of the Electronic Literature Organization Board of Directors.

Canek Zapata (Mexico) is the literary publisher of http://brokenenglish.lol and an internet artist who pursued classical studies at UNAM. His work has been widely exhibited.

Carolina Gainza (Chile) is Phd in Hispanic Languages and Literatures. Subsecretary of the Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation in Chile.

Claudia Kozak (Argentina) is Full Professor and Researcher (Universidad de Buenos Aires-CONICET). She studies el-lit with emphasis in Latin American and decolonial contexts.

David Thomas Henry Wright (Australia), an Associate Professor at Nagoya University and co-editor of The Digital Review, has won multiple international literary prizes.

Doreen A. Ríos (Mexico) is an independent curator and researcher based in Mexico City specialised in digital art, post-digital practices, and new materialities.

Friedrich W. Block (Germany), Director of the Brueckner-Kuehner Foundation and the Kunsttempel gallery in Kassel, Germany, has been curating the POESIS project on digital and media poetry since 1992.

Giovanna di Rosario (Italy and Spain) teaches at the department of Design, Polytechnic of Milan and is the director of HStudies Research Group.

Hugo van Kemenade (UK and Finland) is the co-organiser of National Novel Generation Month (NaNoGenMo), a developer of open-source software, researcher of words, and former builder of Twitter bots.

Judith Okonkwo (Nigeria/UK), a Technology Evangelist and Business Psychologist, is the founder of Imìsí 3D, an ecosystem developer for the extended reality technologies across Africa.

Lai-Tze Fan (Canada), Assistant Professor in Technology and Social Change at the University of Waterloo, Canada, is an Editor of electronic book review and the digital review.

Leonardo Flores (USA) is a hackeur who served as President of the ELO (2019-2022), steering committee for the Red de Literatura Electrónica Latinoamericana, and co-editor of The Electronic Literature Collection, Volume 3, and Antología Lit(e)Lat.

Mohammad Sanajleh (Jordan) is widely acknowledged to be the first Arabic writer of a hypertext novel, Zilal Al-Wahid (Shadows of the One, 2001). He is also Tech writer and editor @ https://www.aljazeera.net/

Monika Górska-Olesińska (Poland) holds a Ph.D. in Humanities from the Jagiellonian University, and is Assistant Professor at the Institute of Contemporary Culture, University of Lodz.

Nanditi Khilnani (India) is co-founder of Ajaibghar, a Creative Tech Agency in India, and co-instigator of dra.ft, a long-term research project exploring emergent ideas of text through collaborative experimentation & community building.

Nohelia Meza (Mexico and UK) is a researcher in Latin American Digital Literature and Culture.

Odile Farge (France) is a Ph.D. in information and communication sciences, a researcher at the PLIDAM (INaLCO University - Sorbonne Paris-Cité), at the UNESCO ITEN Chair, and member of ORBICOM (UQAM).

Reham Hosny (Egypt and UK) is a scholar and author of electronic literature, the co-author of the first Arabic artificial intelligence novel Al-Barrah. She is a board member of the Electronic Literature Organization and director of the arabicelit initiative.

Rejane Rocha (Brazil) is professor at the Federal University of São Carlos/Brazil and a researcher at CNPq, coordinating the Brazilian Digital Literature Observatory.

Zach Whalen (USA) is an Associate Professor of Digital Studies at the University of Mary Washington where he researches and teaches courses in electronic literature, video game studies, creative coding, and comics.

Zuzana Husárová (Slovakia) is an author and researcher of experimental and electronic literature across various media, and teaches at Comenius University (SR) and Masaryk University (CR). A 2011 Fulbright scholar at MIT in the USA, she is an editor of Glosolália magazine.

Fellows

Alessandro Miguez Moreira (Brazil) is Master in Computer Engineering / Mobile Computing.

Eoin Murray (UK) is a Lecturer in Creative Writing at Falmouth University researching gender, utopia, and horror in video games.

Jessica Gray (USA) is an UI Designer & Front-End Dev based in Orlando, Florida.

The Electronic Literature Lab at Washington State University Vancouver, directed by Dene Grigar, handled the metadata for the video playthroughs.
